questions.question: Explain the difference between tandem repeats and interspersed repeats. / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • Explain the difference between tandem repeats and interspersed repeats.
  • Tandem repeats: DNA sequences repeated one after another in a head-to-tail
  • fashion (e.g., AAT-AAT-AAT).
  • Interspersed repeats: DNA sequences (like transposons/retrotransposons) that
  • are scattered at different locations throughout the genome.

questions.question: How does having minimal non-coding DNA help prokaryotes adapt to their environment? / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • How does having minimal non-coding DNA help prokaryotes adapt to
  • their environment?
  • It allows for a compact genome , which enables rapid replication and cell
  • division. This metabolic efficiency (less energy spent on non -essentials) allows
  • them to multiply quickly and exploit favourable conditions. This energy
  • conservation is a major competitive advantage, especially in resource -poor
  • environments where they must compete with other microbes for a limited supply
  • of nutrients.
  • [Valuation: (2 marks) for linking minimal non -coding DNA to rapid
  • replication/metabolic efficiency.]
  • [A] /
  • [CO2]

questions.question: Briefly list at least two significant differences between the structure or organization of the mitochondrial genome and the nuclear genome of eukaryotic cells / [CO1]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • Briefly list at least two significant differences between the structure or
  • organization of the mitochondrial genome and the nuclear genome of
  • eukaryotic cells
  • Any two of the following, explained clearly:
  • o Structure: Mitochondrial (mt) genome is circular, while the nuclear
  • genome consists of linear chromosomes.
  • o Size: mt genome is very small (~16.5 kb in humans), while the nuclear
  • genome is very large (~3.2 Gb).
  • o Gene Density: mt genome is gene-dense with very few introns, while
  • the nuclear genome is mostly non-coding with many introns.
  • o Packaging: mt genome lacks histones , while the nuclear genome is
  • packaged by histones into chromatin.
  • o Inheritance: mt genome is typically maternally inherited, while the
  • nuclear genome is inherited from both parents.
  • [Valuation: (2 marks) for the first clear comparative point. (2 marks) for the
  • second clear comparative point. (1 mark per point if only listed without
  • comparison).]

questions.question: Using the lac operon as an example, outline its structure and explain how it regulates gene expression in response to the presence or absence of lactose. / [CO2]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • Using the lac operon as an example, outline its structure and explain how
  • it regulates gene expression in response to the presence or absence of lactose.
  • Structure: (1 mark) Composed of a Promoter (P) , Operator (O) , and three
  • structural genes ( lacZ, lacY, lacA ). A separate regulator gene ( lacI) codes for a
  • repressor protein.
  • Lactose: (1 mark) The repressor protein binds to the operator , physically
  • blocking RNA polymerase from transcribing the structural genes (genes are OFF).
  • Lactose Present: (2 marks) Allolactose (an inducer derived from lactose) binds
  • to the repressor protein (1 mark). This changes the repressor's shape, causing it
  • to detach from the operator . RNA polymerase can then transcribe the genes
  • (genes are ON) (1 mark).
  • [Valuation: As per the mark breakdown.]
  • [A] /
  • [CO2]

questions.question: Analyze why SV40 is widely used as a model organism in molecular biology and cancer research. / [CO3]

  • and cancer research.

questions.question: Explain how comparative genomics can reveal evolutionary divergence among species. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • Explain how comparative genomics can reveal evolutionary divergence
  • among species.
  • Core Concept of Comparison:
  • Comparative genomics involves comparing the complete genomes ("instruction
  • books") of different species. Evolutionary divergence is revealed by analyzing the
  • similarities and differences in the DNA code. (1 Mark)
  • Role of Homology (Orthologs):
  • By comparing homologous sequences or orthologs (genes in different species
  • inherited from a single ancestral gene), scientists can track divergence. The number
  • of differences (mutations) that have accumulated between the orthologs (like
  • human and chimp myoglobin) indicates how much the species have diverged since
  • they split from that common ancestor. (1 Mark)
  • Role of Gene Duplication (Paralogs):
  • For explaining paralogs as a mechanism for divergence. Gene duplication creates
  • paralogs (related genes within one species) . This allows one copy to keep the
  • original job, while the second copy is "free" to mutate and evolve a new function.
  • This creation of new functions (e.g., alpha- and beta-globin) is a major way species
  • diverge and develop new traits. (1 Mark)
  • Role of Pseudogenes (Fossil Genes):
  • For explaining pseudogenes as evidence of common ancestry before divergence.
  • Finding the same "fossil" gene (pseudogene) in the same location in two different
  • species is strong evidence. The "only logical explanation" is that the gene "broke"
  • in a common ancestor , and both species inherited the already-broken gene before
  • they diverged. (1 Mark)
  • /[CO4]
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025

questions.question: Compare and contrast cladograms, phylograms, and chronograms. / [CO4] [4x8 = 32]
questions.solution_html:
• Ans:
  • Compare and contrast cladograms, phylograms, and chronograms.
  • Commonality: (1 mark) All three are types of phylogenetic trees that show
  • evolutionary relationships (topology).
  • • Cladogram: (1 mark) Only shows the branching pattern
  • (relationships). Branch lengths have no meaning and are arbitrary.
  • • Phylogram: (1 mark) Branch lengths are proportional to the amount of
  • evolutionary change (e.g., number of nucleotide substitutions).
  • • Chronogram: (1 mark) Branch lengths are proportional to actual
  • evolutionary time (e.g., in millions of years), often calibrated using fossil
  • data or molecular clocks.
  • /[CO4]
  • [4x8=32]
